Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough): Discussed integration approach for Verdance clinical assistant; tradeoffs between Hosted/Dedicated/Private; integration surface (SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters), gateway for rate limiting/quotas, and observability/tracing hooks. Action items captured.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, um, quick intros and then we'll jump into how Redwood would fit into Verdance's stack
[00:08] Maya: thanks Jordan, i'm maya, CTO, quick note we have tight compliance needs—PHI scope—so that will guide whether we do hosted or private
[00:15] Jordan: yeah totally, thanks for flagging that up front, we usually look at three patterns: hosted API, dedicated reserved pools, or private (VPC/on-prem). each has tradeoffs on isolation, latency, and ops overhead
[00:28] Priya: to add, from an integration pov the SDKs are straightforward, we support direct REST and client libs; we also provide adapters for LangChain and LlamaIndex, though sometimes the name comes through as "LamaIndex" in auto transcripts so docs clarify. there are examples for python and node
[00:47] Leo: curious—how invasive are those adapters? we use a lot of LlamaIndex pipelines and custom retrievers, don't want to rework the codebase too much
[00:56] Priya: good q, most customers wire in the Redwood client at the LLM / generation layer, for retrieval we recommend plugging our embedding endpoint and serving embeddings to your vector DB. for LlamaIndex we provide a small connector that implements the llm api surface; you should be able to swap-in with minimal glue
[01:15] Ethan: and how about rate limits? we need per-tenant quotas, burst protection, and a hard cap for some internal services
[01:23] Carlos: that is where the gateway/proxy pattern is handy—either you run our lightweight proxy (open-source sample) in your infra which enforces per-tenant rate limits and quotas, or you use a managed route in Redwood Dedicated with config-driven throttles. both support leaky-bucket and token-bucket semantics
[01:39] Anya: for security, we need KMS integration, SAML SSO, and audit logs with token-level tracing if possible; also need guarantees on data-at-rest encryption and retention controls
[01:50] Jordan: yep, we support customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated; hosted customers can use Redwood-managed KMS but we also offer bring-your-own-key for Dedicated with HSM support. audit logs and per-request traces are available via our console and can stream to your SIEM (we have examples for Splunk and Datadog)
[02:08] Maya: what's the overhead of running Private? we don't have a big infra team to manage complex installs
[02:15] Priya: great point, Private can be run in a "managed on VPC" mode where Redwood handles control plane updates and you host inference nodes in your VPC, or full on-prem where you operate both control and data plane. the managed-VPC reduces ops, Dedicated sits in the middle—reserved capacity in our cloud but isolated to you
[02:33] Leo: performance concerns: we need sub-200ms p95 for short prompt generation (single-turn clinical suggestions) — is that realistic on Dedicated vs Hosted?
[02:42] Priya: we typically meet low-latency SLOs on Dedicated due to pinned GPU pools and performance tuning (optimized kernels, KV cache, continuous batching). hosted can also hit it depending on model and region but variability is higher. we can run a benchmark POC to validate your exact prompt set
[03:00] Ethan: about KV cache and prefix cache—does Redwood expose controls? we have long multi-turn conversations and warm caches are important
[03:08] Priya: yes, runtime exposes cache lifetime settings, and you can configure prefix caching on per-model routes. note that some of this is automatic—our smart batching and KV cache heuristics maintain TTLs but we give you knobs for critical paths
[03:24] Anya: any quantization or model variants we should be worried about affecting fidelity? clinical correctness is priority
[03:31] Jordan: we'd recommend trying a 16-bit or 8-bit quantized variant only in non-critical flows; for clinical suggestions we usually pin to a validated model and monitor regen quality. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles by workload, but we surface risk and quality regressions to you
[03:50] Maya: integrations question—we use an internal gateway to handle auth; would we need to run Redwood proxy or can we integrate directly into our gateway?
[03:58] Carlos: you can do either—Direct integration: call Redwood API from your gateway and enforce auth there. Proxy option: run a small sidecar that handles advanced routing, per-tenant quotas, and local caching. proxy reduces round trips for some patterns and helps with burst smoothing
[04:15] Leo: does the SDK stream token events for observability? we want to correlate latency to token-level costs and errors
[04:21] Priya: yes we support streaming responses and emit token-level metrics; observability hooks include per-request token counts, duration, model id, route tags, and traces that link to the console. note: some of the streaming metadata varies slightly across language SDKs right now (we're improving parity)
[04:42] Maya: on compliance, do you provide SOC 2 and pen test reports? we need those to move forward with pilot
[04:49] Jordan: we have SOC 2 Type II and can share redacted penetration test summaries. for private/on-prem we also provide deployment hardening guides. we'll include the security pack in the follow-up docs
[05:01] Ethan: curious about cost controls—if we do hosted, how do we avoid surprise bills during unexpected traffic spikes?
[05:07] Jordan: two levers—rate limits/quotas at the route/gateway layer, and budget alerts in the console. Dedicated also gives predictable unit economics since you commit capacity; we also have automatic fallback policies to lower-cost model variants if you hit budget thresholds
[05:24] Anya: audit log retention—does Redwood hold logs for the length we need? we may need 7 years for certain records though that's extreme
[05:31] Carlos: retention windows are configurable for Private/Dedicated; hosted has tiers for retention (30/90/365 days) as an add-on. long-term archived logs can be exported to your S3 or GCS with encryption at rest
